mcqs.question: Why can the `::` zero-compression shorthand appear at most once in a valid IPv6 address?
options: Because IPv6 addresses can only contain one colon pair by hardware limitation
Because if it appeared twice, the address would be ambiguous — there would be no way to determine how many zero hextets each `::` represents
Because using it twice would exceed the maximum address length
Because the second occurrence is reserved for the subnet prefix specifically
mcqs.explanation: The restriction exists purely to preserve unambiguous parsing: with two `::` occurrences, there'd be no way to know how many zero groups belong to each one. There's no hardware colon limit (option 1), address length isn't affected by using the shorthand (option 3), and there's no reserved second-use rule for prefixes (option 4).

mcqs.question: An IPv6 interface has just been enabled with no DHCPv6 or SLAAC configuration yet. Does it have any address at all?
options: No — like IPv4, an unconfigured interface has no address until DHCP or manual configuration runs
Yes — every IPv6 interface automatically gets a link-local (fe80::/10) address, valid for on-link operations, independent of any other configuration
Yes, but only a global unicast address assigned by the ISP automatically
No — IPv6 interfaces require at least a unique local address to be manually configured first
mcqs.explanation: IPv6 interfaces self-assign a link-local address automatically the moment they come up, regardless of any router or DHCPv6 server being present — this is a deliberate IPv6 design choice, unlike IPv4. Global unicast addresses require external allocation (option 3 false), and there's no manual unique-local requirement before link-local exists (option 4 false); IPv4's behavior (option 1) doesn't carry over to IPv6.

mcqs.question: IPv6 addresses are four times longer than IPv4 addresses, yet routers often process IPv6 headers faster. What explains this?
options: IPv6 headers are fixed-size and drop the header checksum and in-header fragmentation fields that IPv4 routers had to process on every packet
IPv6 packets are always smaller in total size than IPv4 packets
IPv6 routers use a fundamentally different, faster physical transmission medium
IPv6 headers actually contain fewer address bits than IPv4 despite appearances
mcqs.explanation: The speed gain comes from header simplification, not address size: dropping the checksum (recomputed at every hop in IPv4) and moving fragmentation out of the base header reduces per-packet router work, even though the addresses themselves are longer. IPv6 packets aren't inherently smaller (option 2), there's no different physical medium implied by the protocol (option 3), and IPv6 addresses are genuinely 128 bits, not fewer (option 4 false).
